Its elevation and inclination must be so arranged that it corresponds to the description of a Pythagorean right-angled triangle <note>original: "pythagoricum trigonum orthogonium"</note>. That is, if the length is divided into five parts, the head of the screw should be raised by three of those parts; thus the distance from the perpendicular to its lower openings <note>original: "imas nares"</note> will be four parts. The method by which this should be done is shown in its diagram described at the end of the book.

<margin>
a. The screw <note>original: "coclea"</note> erected according to the ratio of the Pythagorean triangle <note>original: "trigoni pythagorici"</note>.
b. The beams <note>original: "tigna"</note> in which the screw turns.

<note>A woodcut illustration depicts an Archimedean screw </note><note>original: "coclea"</note> used for irrigation or drainage. The device consists of a wooden shaft with an internal spiral encased in a cylinder, tilted at an angle. The lower end is submerged in water, and the upper end is supported by a tall wooden pillar labeled 'b'. A large treadwheel labeled 'd' is attached to the center of the shaft, allowing humans to turn the device by treading on its rungs. Water is shown being lifted through the screw and discharging from the top into a wooden trough or basin. The letter 'a' labels the main body of the screw.

Regarding this subject, these are the machines <note>original: "organa"</note> made for drawing water <note>original: "hauriendam aquam"</note>, the methods by which they are completed, and the means by which they receive motion to provide rotations <note>original: "uersationibus"</note> for endless uses,

<summary>This page explains the mechanical operation and geometric positioning of the Archimedean screw. It specifies using the 3:4:5 Pythagorean ratio for its inclination to ensure efficient water lifting.</summary>
<keywords>Archimedean screw, Pythagorean triangle, hydraulic engineering, treadwheel, water lifting, Vitruvius, Roman technology</keywords>
